clinicalPearls: A rare congenital malformation of the mitral subvalvar apparatus in which papillary muscles connect directly, or through short thickened chordae, to a bridge of fibrous tissue along the leaflet edge
The resulting 'hammock' arrangement restricts leaflet motion and disrupts normal coaptation, causing mitral stenosis, regurgitation, or a mixed lesion
Part of the spectrum of congenital mitral inflow anomalies and often associated with other left heart obstructive lesions
Typically presents in infancy or childhood with breathlessness, poor feeding or failure to thrive, and features of pulmonary venous congestion, though milder forms may present later
Careful echocardiographic assessment of the whole mitral apparatus, including papillary muscles and chordae, is essential to define the mechanism
Distinguishing arcade from other congenital mitral lesions such as parachute valve and supravalvar ring guides surgical planning
Management is surgical when the lesion is significant, favouring valve repair where feasible, with replacement reserved for valves not amenable to repair
reference.pathophysiology: In a mitral arcade the normal delicate chordal support of the mitral leaflets is replaced by direct or near-direct insertion of the papillary muscles into a thickened fibrous ridge running along the free edge of the leaflets. This tethering fixes the leaflets in a curtain-like or hammock configuration that limits their excursion and prevents proper coaptation, so blood flow across the valve is obstructed and, or, the valve leaks. The consequent rise in left atrial pressure is transmitted to the pulmonary circulation, producing pulmonary venous congestion and, if long-standing, pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital mitral stenosis from other causes
Shone complex with multilevel left heart obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography with detailed assessment of leaflets, chordae, and papillary muscles
Transoesophageal echocardiography for finer definition of the subvalvar apparatus
Three-dimensional echocardiography to display the arcade morphology for surgical planning
Cardiac MRI or CT to clarify anatomy and associated left heart lesions when needed
Assessment of pulmonary artery pressure by echocardiography or right heart catheterisation
redFlags: Heart failure or failure to thrive in an infant with a congenital mitral lesion
Severe mitral stenosis or regurgitation with pulmonary venous congestion
Established pulmonary hypertension from chronic obstruction
Multilevel left heart obstruction indicating a Shone-type complex
reference.prognosis: The outlook depends on the severity of valve dysfunction and associated lesions; timely repair can give good results, but the abnormal apparatus makes durable repair challenging and some patients ultimately require valve replacement.
pitfalls: Diagnosing mitral stenosis without recognising the abnormal subvalvar arcade responsible
Confusing an arcade with a parachute valve or supravalvar ring, which alters surgical strategy
Failing to look for associated left heart obstructive lesions
Underestimating the difficulty of achieving a durable repair of the malformed apparatus
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease
management: Definitive treatment is surgical, with mitral valve repair of the abnormal subvalvar apparatus where feasible or valve replacement when durable repair is not possible
Medical therapy of pulmonary venous congestion and heart failure with diuretics and afterload reduction to stabilise symptoms before surgery
Nutritional support for failure to thrive in infants with feeding difficulty
Detailed echocardiographic assessment of the whole mitral apparatus to define the mechanism and distinguish arcade from parachute valve and supravalvar ring, guiding surgical planning
Monitor for and manage pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain
Screen for associated left-heart obstructive lesions and attend to oral health and endocarditis prevention
Paediatric cardiology and congenital cardiac surgical referral with long-term follow-up for recurrent or residual valve dysfunction
